html:
A short book by the Roman historian Tacitus, written around 98 CE, about the lands and peoples of Germania beyond the Rhine and Danube. It is the fullest ancient account of the early Germanic peoples.

The first half describes the Germans in general: their land, their weapons and war bands, their assemblies, their gods, their faithful marriages and their love of drink and gambling. The second half goes tribe by tribe, from the Cherusci and Chatti near the Rhine to peoples on the Baltic who gathered amber.

Tacitus probably never went there. He used earlier writers, including the lost German Wars of Pliny the Elder. His Germans are partly a mirror for Rome: brave, simple and free, set against Roman luxury and servility. He follows Caesar's contrast between Gauls and Germans in the Gallic War.

A single manuscript survived, found in a German abbey and brought to Italy in the 1400s. German humanists hailed it as proof of a noble national past. Much later the Nazis seized on its claim that the Germans were an unmixed people. One historian called it among the most dangerous books ever written.
sum: A short book by the Roman historian Tacitus, written around 98 CE, about the lands and peoples of Germania beyond the Rhine and Danube. It is the fullest ancient account of the early Germanic peoples.
